answer:
1. The animation shows how inflation wears down a fixed income. An illustrative retiree, Carl, starts in January 1966 with a check that buys 10 crates of goods. His check grows only about 2% a year, while prices rise 6.38% a year, which the animation calls the fastest stretch.

2. The check stays nearly flat while prices keep climbing, so the crates it buys disappear one by one. By year 13 about half are gone. By year 20 only about 4 of the 10 crates are left. The animation says he has less buying power on all 20 of 20 anniversaries. A small line chart for Ruth, another illustrative retiree, shows a different path that is "back above in early years" and then falls. The frames don't make clear how Ruth's check differs from Carl's.

3. A payout that rises more slowly than prices loses real value every year, even if the dollar amount never drops. In this one historical case, the loss was large over 20 years. The animation labels itself "US only · history, not a forecast," so it doesn't claim this will happen again.

4. The animation doesn't tell the viewer to do anything. A viewer could reasonably take away that they should check whether an annuity payout adjusts for inflation. For me, at 64 and comparing two payout options, that means asking whether either one rises with prices. It also means weighing a lower starting payment with inflation adjustment against a higher flat one. That is my reading of the animation, not something it says.

5. The advice in 4 is my own conclusion. The animation only shows the erosion of buying power in one illustrative, historical case and says it is not a forecast. It doesn't recommend a product or a choice.
